editorial:
Imagine it is the early 80s and the world of cable TV is like the Wild West. You get to follow Bob Surge, a guy who owns a video store chain and wants to feel young and rebellious again. He gets a public access channel and hires Max Loom to run the show. Max doesn't play by the rules and turns the station into a wild, edgy playground. From crazy presenters like Teddy Whazz to weird segments that push the limits, the vibe is high-energy and chaotic. It feels like a party where anyone can grab the microphone, making the whole experience feel fresh and spontaneous.

What really makes this work is the clash between the creative chaos of the crew and the grumpy people trying to shut them down. The pacing is quick, and the acting feels natural for a TV movie of this era. While it might feel a bit dated in some spots, the fight against the censorship group Cable Concern adds a nice bit of tension. If you like stories about underdogs and media madness, you should definitely check this out.
endingExplained: The dream eventually crashes when the pressure from the right-wing censorship group becomes too much to handle. Bob Surge loses his nerve and chooses safety and money over the rebellion he claimed to love. The wild energy of the station is killed off by corporate rules and strict guidelines. You see the gang get pushed out as the channel becomes boring and safe, proving that the corporate world usually wins over creative freedom.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves stories about the early days of television and fighting the man.
